Four failures, one blind spot

An evening of “the server is fine” while the screen said otherwise — what actually broke each time, and the one thing all four had in common.

Post-mortem · 17 Sep 2026 · katomia / kpay

The thread. Four separate faults, and in every one of them the evidence that would have identified it in seconds sat somewhere I could not reach: a Cloudflare build log, a browser tab, an address bar, a config file on a phone. Every time, I checked the things I could reach, found them healthy, and said so — which was true, useless, and misleading in roughly equal measure.

01What actually broke

The deploy that never ran ~1 hour

Moving the API alias to api.katomia.com silently broke the front-end deploy. build-static.sh computed the service-binding name as ${ALIAS%%.*} — “the first label of the alias's workers.dev host” — which was true only while the alias was a workers.dev host. The custom domain made it yield api, and no Worker is called that.

Where the error wasCloudflare's build log: Service binding 'HAPI' references Worker 'api' which was not found [10143]
What I could seeGitHub Actions green · commit correct on pilot · both dists matching their source

The patch that never saved ~30 min

A patch script hit a failed assertion and exited before its write step, so five edits were lost while the explanatory note describing them was saved. The page then documented behaviour it did not have. I reported the change as shipped because the commit existed.

Where the error wasNowhere — the script exited 0-ish and the commit looked ordinary
What I could seeA commit, a green build, a note in the diff saying the right things

The stale tab ~20 min

A browser left open across a deploy keeps running the JavaScript it loaded. Nothing tells it otherwise, and nothing tells the person looking at it either.

Where the error wasIn the tab. Invisible from the server, invisible from the repo
What I could seeThe correct bundle being served, and every endpoint at 200

The missing trailing slash ~45 min, and the one that finally paid

The dashboard resolves the API base as new URL('../') — which is /future/ from /future/v3/ and / from /future/v3. The router matched both forms and served the page for each, so the slash-less URL loaded a working-looking dashboard whose every call went to the site root, which 302s to the home page. The page parsed HTML as JSON.

Where the error wasThe address bar. I probed the correct path perfectly, 10/10 and 12/12 clean
What ended itOne improved error message, first time it ran: got a web page, not data, from /?…action=signers

02The pattern

These are four different bugs — a shell expansion, a script exiting early, browser caching, a URL normalisation. They do not share a cause. They share a diagnostic shape:

 Could I see it?What I concluded instead
Cloudflare build logNo — token is read-only and cannot see Workers Builds“the deploy must be slow”
The browser's consoleNo“the server is healthy, so it must be cache”
The URL being visitedNo — I assumed the one in an old screenshot“I cannot reproduce it”
A config file on a phoneNocorrect, but only after three claims had expired

In each case I had a green signal from the half of the system I could observe, and treated it as evidence about the whole. That is the actual failure, and it is mine: a check that cannot fail on the broken half is not evidence, and reporting it as reassurance is worse than saying nothing.

What worked

Exactly one thing broke the deadlock, and it was not more server-side probing. It was making the client say what it tried and what came back. That message was written an hour before it was needed, for a different reason, and it identified the fault on its first run. Every hour of this evening's investigation could have been replaced by it.

03What is already fixed

Errors that name the call done

getJson now reads the body before deciding. A non-2xx carries its status, the path and the start of the response; a 2xx that is not JSON quotes what did arrive and says a sign-in or error page would look like this. The two likeliest causes both send HTML, and both used to surface as Unexpected token '<' — a message that names the symptom and hides the cause.

The page notices when it is stale done

It compares the build stamp it booted with against build-info.json on each refresh and offers a reload once when they differ. Its own failure is swallowed deliberately: a courtesy must not take down the thing it decorates.

The trailing slash, at both ends done

The router redirects /future/v3, /future/v3/help and /future/v3/help/business to their slash forms, preserving the query string — the convention /qa already followed. And the page derives its base from a known anchor in its own path rather than ../, so it survives any host that serves it without one.

The service-binding name is declared done

Not derived from a hostname. A Worker's name and the address it answers on are independent facts, and the build script now says so rather than assuming.

A clash detector, and both build variants done

ops/clash-check.sh reports whether the base branch moved and separates a source clash from a generated one. build-static.sh with no argument builds both dists — the stale dist-gcp caught two sessions in one day, which is a trap in the tool rather than two mistakes.

04What is still open

A deploy that fails after CI is green must be loud next

This is the biggest remaining hole. The katui workflow already has a smoke job meant to curl the live routes after a push, and it did not catch an hour of failed deploys. Give it something version-shaped to assert: build-info.json already carries source_sha, so “the bundle in git” and “the bundle being served” can be compared rather than assumed equal. Roughly ten lines, and it closes the single worst case in this list. kpayuk and kmigrate have the same blind spot and have not been bitten yet.

Patch scripts must not be able to half-apply soon

The lost-edits case was a script whose write came after its last assertion. Any edit script should verify its result after writing — grep for what it claimed to add — rather than trusting that reaching the end meant success. This is a habit, not a tool, and it is mine to hold.

Put the URL where a report can carry it cheap

Three of the four cases would have been shorter if the first message had included the exact URL being visited. The page could show its own resolved API base in the raw-links row it already has, so a screenshot carries it without anyone having to think of it.

05On posting front-end logs to the backend

This is the obvious answer to “I cannot see the client”, and it has bitten this estate before. Worth being precise about which part is dangerous, because the useful part and the dangerous part are separable.

The trap

An open POST /log that accepts arbitrary text is an unauthenticated write endpoint with unbounded storage, it will faithfully record whatever happens to be in scope — tokens, account ids, query strings, a signing key someone pasted into a form — and a log viewer that renders it becomes stored XSS aimed squarely at an admin. That is three separate incidents waiting in one convenience.

The version worth having

Do not ship logs. Ship a fingerprint: on a failure, the page reports a small fixed-shape record — { page, buildSha, apiBase, action, httpStatus, bodyKind } — where bodyKind is one of a handful of enum values (json / html / empty), never the body itself. No free text, so nothing can leak through it and nothing can be rendered as markup. Every one of tonight's four would have been identified by that record alone.

Even that should be rate-limited per IP, capped in size, and written to a store the admin page renders as text, never HTML. And it is worth noting the cheaper alternative first: the improved error message already puts all of that on the screen, so a screenshot carries it. The endpoint only buys you the cases where nobody is looking — which, for a dashboard meant to run unattended overnight, is a real category, but not today's.

06The rule I should have been following

Say which half I checked. “All three endpoints return 200 through the front-end path, ten consecutive calls clean” is a useful sentence. “The server is fine” is the same information with the boundary sanded off, and it invites exactly the wrong conclusion. When the person looking at the screen and the person reading the logs disagree, the screen is the one with the fault in front of it — and the next question should be what does it say, exactly, not let me check the server again.
